summary:
Jeju stands under the national framework of South Korea. Consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal and gender identity is not criminalised in civilian life; the criminalising provision in force is Military Criminal Act article 92-6, which punishes consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment. The Constitutional Court upheld the article in 2023, and enforcement has been punitive rather than dormant: a 2017 military operation led to criminal charges against 32 personnel, and a gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

That exclusion produced the sharpest documented harm against a trans person in the country. Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel treated the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap, and she died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021; the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty in March 2024.

Legal gender recognition is available on Jeju. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that conditioning gender change on surgery is against the law and that court guidelines once requiring surgery now serve as reference rather than criteria. The ruling removed the surgical prerequisite for registered-sex change nationwide, including in Jeju, and the wire report records no specific case on the island.

Public restroom use carries an enforceable right. On 22 July 2024 a Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against the state on a claim of 3 million won, holding that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female, whose family-register gender change had been approved by a court in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights, and that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. These national rulings govern Jeju, and the article reports no specific incident there.

A 2021 survey by the National Human Rights Commission of Korea of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% avoided facilities out of fear. Visitors should also expect no recognition of their relationships: South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. No comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Violence concentrates at public events. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, and organisers later filed charges against pastors while accusing police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. Police presence of that scale is a marker of the threat level around Pride, not of its absence.

Everyday hostility is documented at high rates. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates, that 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, and that among those recommended it 65.4% reported harm and 94% psychological trauma; a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults had faced harsh discrimination in the past year. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street in the absence of a nondiscrimination bill.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, arguing that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.
localsOnly:
Restroom avoidance is entrenched among residents. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early, and researchers urged legal and institutional reform for safer school environments.

Legal gender recognition has loosened beyond the surgery question. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender individuals with minor children can have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent that uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors; a 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children. The Yeongdong court added on 8 May 2024 that every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity.

Relationship recognition remains narrow. A landmark 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance short of marriage. Because no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity, protection depends on individual litigation; an NGO won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017, the government appealed onward, and Human Rights Watch described years of bureaucratic obstruction. LGBTI organisations can nonetheless register.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Jeju-specific evidence is sourced for any of the findings above. The Korea Times article reports no specific restroom incident on the island and the Yonhap wire reports no specific gender-recognition case there, so whether article 92-6 has been enforced against personnel stationed on Jeju, and whether Jeju residents have litigated restroom or facility access, remains unresolved rather than established as absent.

The restroom judgment is dated inconsistently across the available material: the parent framework dates a final ruling to 2 July 2024 at the Seoul Central District Court, while the Korea Times item of 22 July 2024 describes an appellate court dismissing the state's appeal. Whether these are first and second instance of the same case, and which court holds the file, is unresolved.

Hate-crime provisions covering gender identity, local anti-discrimination ordinances on Jeju, and the treatment of marker changes on Jeju-issued identity documents are not sourced in this inventory. Facility availability, including gendered restroom and shelter provision on the island, is likewise not documented here.
